## What we covered

Humana's exit from the ACA exchanges and why an insurer has to understand its
risk pool. Then the three ideas that turn "I don't like risk" into a dollar
figure: the certainty equivalent, the risk premium, and willingness to pay for
insurance. We worked the $100,000 example one step at a time. Then what moves
the risk premium, why high-risk pools struggle, how plan design sorts people,
and a first pass at unraveling that came out of a question. We skipped the
in-class problem for time.

## Key points

- The certainty equivalent is an amount of money. It's the wealth you would
  accept with certainty and feel the same as you do facing the gamble. It is a
  point on the wealth axis, not a payment. You find it by taking the expected
  utility and inverting the utility function to get back to dollars.
- Expected utility only uses the two endpoints, healthy and sick. Where you sit
  on the line between them is set by the probability of illness. The curve
  doesn't enter until you ask what certain amount gives the same utility.
- The risk premium is expected wealth minus the certainty equivalent. It's what
  you would give up to make the uncertainty go away, and it's positive whenever
  the utility curve is concave.
- Willingness to pay for insurance is the expected cost of illness plus the
  risk premium. The expected cost is the actuarially fair premium, what an
  insurer would charge if it charged exactly its cost. "Willingness to pay"
  shows up twice in this material, so always ask willingness to pay for what.
- Expected wealth is starting wealth minus expected cost. In the small example,
  $100 to start, $80 cost if sick, a coin flip: expected wealth 60, expected
  cost 40, and you'd pay a little more than 40 because you don't like the risk.
- The worked example, log utility, $100,000, a 25 percent chance of a $20,000
  loss: expected wealth 95,000; expected utility 11.45714; certainty equivalent
  exp(11.45714), which is 94,574; risk premium about 426; expected cost 5,000;
  willingness to pay 5,426. Keep several decimals before you exponentiate,
  because a 0.01 difference in utility is a real difference in dollars.
- Exponentiating undoes a log and nothing else. If the utility function is a
  square root, you square to invert it.
- Willingness to pay is a maximum, not what anyone volunteers. The expected-cost
  part is a transfer, you pay the insurer and the insurer pays the provider. The
  risk premium is where the insurer's profit can come from: risk-averse buyers,
  a risk-neutral insurer, everyone better off.
- Three things move the risk premium. More curvature in the utility function
  (more risk aversion) raises it. A larger cost of illness raises it. The
  probability of illness is the odd one out: the risk premium is largest near a
  coin flip and small when illness is nearly certain, because that's where the
  uncertainty is. Willingness to pay keeps rising with the probability, but
  expected cost takes over and the risk premium becomes a small part of it.
- That's the problem with high-risk pools. Everyone in them has a high
  willingness to pay, but almost all of it is expected cost. There's little
  risk premium and so little room for profit, which is one reason they
  struggle.
- Plan design is how an insurer shapes its pool. A low premium with a high
  deductible attracts healthy people; someone who expects to be sick wants
  stability and goes elsewhere. Plans that end up with the sick have a hard
  time surviving.
- Insurers price by plan and by market, not by person. A plan offered in DeKalb
  County has one price for everyone who enrolls in it, and the same insurer
  offers different plans at different prices elsewhere.
- Raising the price after a bad year loses the healthiest enrollees first,
  which leaves the pool sicker and the new price too low again. Repeat and you
  have unraveling, sometimes called a death spiral. Next Tuesday does this
  formally.
- The certainty equivalent isn't special to insurance. It's the standard way
  economists put a dollar value on a policy change in any setting.

## Clarifications

- **The certainty equivalent is a value, not a payment.** This came up several
  times, so once more. The certainty equivalent is a number on the wealth axis.
  The risk premium is a gap between two numbers on that axis, expected wealth
  and the certainty equivalent. Willingness to pay for insurance is a bigger
  gap, from starting wealth down to the certainty equivalent, which is the same
  as expected cost plus the risk premium.
- **The full answer to the worked example.** Willingness to pay is $5,426, the
  $5,000 expected cost plus the $426 risk premium, not either piece on its own.

## Thursday, and the homework

Thursday starts with a short quiz, then the simulation. The quiz can ask you to
compute an expected value, a certainty equivalent, a risk premium, or a
willingness to pay, and to say which direction each of the three determinants
pushes. Quizzes are open note; the time limit is the constraint. Do the
in-class problem from the slides at home first, the $100 and $50 case at three
probabilities, and notice what happens to the risk premium as the probability
rises.

Two traps in the homework 1 data collection on the New Jersey site. Historical
enrollment isn't presented like the rate history; scroll down past the recent
quarters until you see the tabs labeled historical. And quarterly enrollment
counts are the same people each quarter, so don't add quarters together. Pick
one quarter per year or average them.
